statement: To find two straight lines incommensurable, the one in length only, and the other in square also, with an assigned straight line.
heath_proof: Let A be the assigned straight line; thus it is required to find two straight lines incommensurable, the one in length only, and the other in square also, with A. Let two numbers B, C be set out which have not to one another the ratio which a square number has to a square number, that is, which are not similar plane numbers; and let it be contrived that, as B is to C, so is the square on A to the square on D  —for we have learnt how to do this— [X. 6] therefore the square on A is commensurable with the square on D. [X. 6] And, since B has not to C the ratio which a square number has to a square number, therefore neither has the square on A to the square on D the ratio which a square number has to a square number; therefore A is incommensurable in length with D. [X. 9] Let E be taken a mean proportional between A, D; therefore, as A is to D, so is the square on A to the square on E. [V. Def. 9] But A is incommensurable in length with D; therefore the square on A is also incommensurable with the square on E; [X. 11] therefore A is incommensurable in square with E. Therefore two straight lines D, E have been found incommensurable, D in length only, and E in square and of course in length also, with the assigned straight line A.]

10.10
**Statement:** To find two straight lines incommensurable, the one in length only, and the other in square also, with an assigned straight line.

**Step 1.** Let A be the assigned straight line. We are required to find two straight lines, one incommensurable with A in length only, and the other incommensurable with A in square also.

**Step 2.** Construct a straight line B such that the square on B is equal to twice the square on A. This can be done by setting up a right angle and making each of the two sides containing the right angle equal to A; the hypotenuse, by the Pythagorean theorem [1.47], has its square equal to the sum of the squares on the two sides, that is, equal to twice the square on A. Let B be this hypotenuse.

**Step 3.** Then the square on B has to the square on A the ratio 2 : 1, which is the ratio of a number to a number. Therefore the square on B is commensurable with the square on A [10.6].

**Step 4.** Now 2 is not a square number, and 1 is a square number, so the ratio 2 : 1 is not the ratio of a square number to a square number. Therefore, by 10.9, B is incommensurable in length with A.

**Step 5.** Since B is incommensurable in length with A, yet the square on B is commensurable with the square on A, B is incommensurable with A in length only [D10.1.1, D10.1.2]. This is the first required line.

**Step 6.** Next, take A and B, and find their mean proportional C, so that A is to C as C is to B [6.13].

**Step 7.** Then the square on C is equal to the rectangle contained by A and B, that is, A : C :: C : B implies the square on C equals the rectangle A by B [6.17].

**Step 8.** Since B is incommensurable in length with A, the ratio of B to A is not the ratio of a number to a number [10.7].

**Step 9.** Now the square on C is to the square on A as B is to A. For since the square on C equals the rectangle A by B, we have the square on C to the square on A equal to (A times B) to (A times A), which equals B to A [6.1].

**Step 10.** Since the ratio of B to A is not the ratio of a number to a number [Step 8], the ratio of the square on C to the square on A is not the ratio of a number to a number either.

**Step 11.** Therefore, by 10.8, the square on C is incommensurable with the square on A, which means C is incommensurable in square with A [D10.1.2]. This is the second required line.

**Step 12.** Therefore we have found B, incommensurable with the assigned straight line A in length only, and C, incommensurable with A in square also, which is what was required to find. Q.E.F.
